person.name: Frei_Otto
person.summary: Frei Otto was a German architect and teacher who developed lightweight structures based on cable nets, membranes, and grids. His work joined experimental models with major public buildings, including the roofs for the Munich Olympic Park and Mannheim's Multihalle.

conclusion: Frei Otto developed cable nets, membranes, and grid shells for buildings that used little material, surface, and energy. The Munich Olympic roofs and Mannheim Multihalle remain prominent examples of this work. His Institute for Lightweight Structures at the University of Stuttgart continues as ILEK.

events.title: Birth in Siegmar
events.description: Frei Paul Otto was born in Siegmar, Germany, to parents who belonged to the [[German Werkbund|German association of artists, architects, and designers]]. His first name, Frei, came from his mother, whose motto was “free.”

German Werkbund.explanation: Founded in 1907, the German Werkbund linked designers, architects, artists, and manufacturers to improve the quality of industrial products and buildings.

events.title: Studies Architecture During War
events.description: In 1943, Frei Otto began studying architecture at the Technical University of Berlin. His studies were interrupted when he was trained and deployed as a fighter pilot during World War II.

events.title: Captivity in Chartres
events.description: Otto was held in a French prisoner-of-war camp in Chartres after his capture near Nuremberg. He helped design several low-cost buildings for the camp using lightweight construction. The stone structure of [[Chartres Cathedral]] provided a daily example of structural lightness.

Chartres Cathedral.explanation: Chartres Cathedral is a major Gothic cathedral in northern France, known for its high stone vaults, flying buttresses, and stained glass.

events.title: Returns to Berlin Studies
events.description: In 1948, Frei Otto resumed architecture studies at the Technical University of Berlin after his release from French captivity. The [[Studienstiftung des deutschen Volkes|Studienstiftung]] supported his studies as a German scholarship foundation.

Studienstiftung des deutschen Volkes.explanation: The Studienstiftung des deutschen Volkes is Germany’s largest scholarship foundation for academically talented students.

events.title: Studies Architecture in America
events.description: In 1950, Frei Otto receives a faculty scholarship for six months of architectural study in the United States. He visits the work of Erich Mendelsohn, Ludwig Mies van der Rohe, Richard Neutra, Frank Lloyd Wright, Eero Saarinen, and engineer Fred Severud. In Severud’s New York office, he sees a model of the suspended roof for the Dorton Arena in Raleigh, North Carolina.

images.caption: Ludwig Mies van der Rohe-designed subdivision
images.creator: Greg

events.title: Begins Marriage With Ingrid Smolla
events.description: Frei Otto marries Ingrid Smolla in 1952. Their marriage lasts until Otto’s death.

events.title: Opens Berlin Studio
events.description: In 1952, Frei Otto opened his own architectural office in Berlin-Zehlendorf. He used the practice to develop proposals for lightweight construction.

events.title: Publishes Das hängende Dach Study
events.description: In 1954, Frei Otto publishes Das hängende Dach, a study of tension structures that carry loads through cables, nets, or membranes. The Dorton Arena model he saw in Fred Severud’s New York office directs his attention to this form of roof. Otto meets tent manufacturer Peter Stromeyer while preparing the study.

images.caption: J.S. Dorton Arena in Raleigh
images.creator: Billie Grace Ward from New York, USA

event_class.title: Das hängende Dach
event_class.impact: The study brings Otto invitations for visiting professorships at American universities.

events.background:
Matthew Nowicki’s Dorton Arena used a saddle-shaped cable-net roof. Two opposing semicircular edge cables carried the net. They crossed at the roof edge. Horizontal steel members anchored in the ground stabilized the cables against one another.

Otto’s research treated cable nets, membranes, and other surfaces that carry force in tension. It was the first comprehensive account of such tensioned surface structures. His connection with Peter Stromeyer during the work gave the research a route into fabrication. Stromeyer’s Konstanz company later made Otto’s tent structures, including the German Pavilion for Expo 67 in Montreal.

background_images.caption: Pavilion of German Federal Republic, on Notre-Dame Island. Montréal, Québec, Canada.
background_images.creator: Laurent Bélanger

events.title: Founds Lightweight Construction Center
events.description: In 1957, Frei Otto founds a development center for [[lightweight construction|lightweight construction]] in Berlin. The approach uses structural forms and materials efficiently. The center supports his models and experiments for roofs that use minimal material.

lightweight construction.explanation: The field seeks structures that do more with less material and energy. Otto pursued it through cable nets, membranes, grids, and physical models.

events.title: Founds Stuttgart Lightweight Structures Institute
events.description: In 1964, Frei Otto founds the Institute for Lightweight Structures at the Technical University of Stuttgart. Researchers there investigate lightweight construction and natural forms.

images.caption: Frei Otto Institute for Lightweight Structures
images.creator: 準建築人手札網站 Forgemind ArchiMedia

events.title: Builds German Pavilion at Expo 67
events.description: In 1967, Frei Otto helps design the German Pavilion for Expo 67 in Montreal with architect Rolf Gutbrod and other collaborators. Peter Stromeyer’s tent-building company fabricates its roof from a network of tensioned cables.

images.caption: Frei Otto German Pavilion at Expo 67
images.creator: bianca.maggio

events.background:
The pavilion included a double-curved roof made as a wooden grid shell. It covered a lecture hall and foyer within the structure. The grid-shell approach was later developed further in the roof design for Munich’s Olympic Park.

Otto’s article dates the Union Internationale des Architectes’ Auguste Perret Prize for the pavilion to 1967. Gutbrod’s article dates that award to 1968.

background_images.caption: Pavilion of German Federal Republic, on Notre-Dame Island. Montréal, Québec, Canada.
background_images.creator: Laurent Bélanger

events.title: Designs Olympic Canopy
events.description: In 1968, Frei Otto worked with Günter Behnisch and the Behnisch & Partner architectural team in Munich on the cable-net roof for the Olympic Park’s main sports venues. The design covered the Olympic Stadium and neighboring facilities with a continuous, transparent canopy supported by suspended steel cables.

images.caption: Frei Otto tensile structures at Munich Olympics
images.creator: Jorge Royan

events.background:
The proposed roof faced unexpected problems because it had to span such large areas. Günter Behnisch brought Frei Otto into the work after those difficulties emerged. The team developed a version of the floating roof Otto had previously conceived for the German Pavilion at Expo 67 in Montreal.

Fritz Leonhardt and Jörg Schlaich led the structural engineering. Otto thought the finished design's edge cables and supporting columns were too heavy for his idea of lightweight construction. Leonhardt and Schlaich prevailed with their requirements for structural safety.

Häuser magazine selected the completed Olympic complex as the best German building of all time in 2002.

background_images.caption: Besichtigung der Dachkonstruktion des Olympia Stadions München mit Begehung.
background_images.creator: Usien

events.title: Completes Mannheim’s Multihalle Grid Shell
events.description: In 1975, Frei Otto developed the structural design for the Multihalle in Mannheim with architects Carlfried Mutschler and Joachim Langner. The project followed their successful competition proposal for the Herzogenriedpark site of the [[Bundesgartenschau|federal garden show]], which called for a covered meeting place and café.

Bundesgartenschau.explanation: The Bundesgartenschau is a national German garden show held in a different city every two years. Mannheim hosted the 1975 edition, for which the Multihalle was built.

event_class.title: Multihalle timber grid shell
event_class.description: A free-form roof uses intersecting timber laths shaped into a double-curved grid shell that carries loads mainly through compression.
event_class.impact: The completed hall becomes the world's largest free-form timber grid-shell structure.

events.title: Leads Stuttgart Research and Teaching
events.description: In 1976, Frei Otto becomes a full professor at the University of Stuttgart. He leads research and teaching through the Institute for Lightweight Structures.

events.title: Continues Work From Warmbronn Studio
events.description: In 1990, Frei Otto becomes emeritus from his professorship at the University of Stuttgart. He continues working from his studio in Warmbronn near Leonberg. His wife Ingrid Smolla and their daughter, architect Christine Otto-Kanstinger, work with him there.

events.title: Dies After Years in Warmbronn
events.description: Increasing blindness restricts Otto’s work in Warmbronn. He remains active in his studio there. He dies in Leonberg on March 9, 2015.
events.background:
The Pritzker Architecture Prize recognized Otto during his lifetime in 2015. Its presentation took place after his death.

Otto’s extensive project archive is held by the Southwest German Archive for Architecture and Civil Engineering in Karlsruhe. In 2016 and 2017, the archive joined Wüstenrot Foundation and ZKM Karlsruhe for the largest exhibition of his work, Frei Otto. Thinking in Models.
